capabilities.target: Supabase Postgres database via service role (execute_sql); bypasses row level security; includes the integration_tokens table
insert into support_messages, visible to the customer who filed the ticket

inputs.source: Developer's direct prompt in the IDE chat ('Show me the latest open support tickets.')
Customer-written ticket message submitted through the public support widget, later read back via execute_sql

elements.name: Supabase Postgres database (service role, RLS bypassed; includes integration_tokens table)
Customer ticket message into agent context

controls.name: IDE client per-call approval prompt showing raw SQL
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the IDE client outside the model and shows the raw SQL, so it does not decay with model capability. It decays with approval volume: developers approve many calls per session, which is the approval-fatigue pattern (SAFE-T1403) that leads to rubber-stamping.

controls.name: Least-privilege database role (no service_role, RLS enforced, no access to integration_tokens)
controls.decay_rationale: A role that enforces RLS and excludes the integration_tokens table makes the sensitive read unreachable regardless of model behavior; it does not decay with capability.

controls.name: Content filter on inserts to customer-visible tables (secret/token pattern detection)
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced outside the model, but encoded or paraphrased secrets can get past pattern-based detection, and new egress channels are not covered automatically.

controls.name: Injection classifier / spotlighting on ticket message content before planning
controls.decay_rationale: The classifier sees content, not intent; multi-turn or obfuscated injection payloads in ticket text can get past it, and it does not scale with a more capable attacker model.

controls.name: Tamper-evident audit log of execute_sql calls tied to approving developer identity
controls.decay_rationale: If enforced at the infrastructure layer (e.g., DB-side logging independent of the agent's own output), it does not decay with model capability; it is detective only and does not prevent the action.

controls.name: Hard per-session/per-hour cap on execute_sql calls
controls.decay_rationale: A hard cap enforced outside the model bounds volume regardless of how persuasive or capable the model is; it narrows rather than prevents, and low-and-slow abuse can stay under it.

controls.name: Pin Supabase MCP server version and verify package integrity
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning and hash verification prevent silent tool redefinition on each invocation; it fails if a new, unpinned server is added without the same control (new_mcp_server trigger).

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): ticket-injected SQL read of integration tokens exfiltrated via customer-visible reply, under an approval-fatigued gate

attack_path.note: Attacker-authored ticket content, retrieved as part of normal ticket processing
Service-role execute_sql, bypassing RLS, can be directed by the ticket content to read the integration_tokens table
Agent inserts the harvested tokens into a support_messages reply visible to the customer who filed the ticket

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Autonomy level raised from A1 to A2/A3/A4, or the per-call approval prompt removed/narrowed in the IDE client config; or approvals-per-session trending upward, confirming fatigue.

evidence.observation: mcp.json launches the Supabase MCP server with an access token and no pinned version, giving the agent's execute_sql tool whatever privileges that token/role carries.

The database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security, and a table of integration tokens sits in the same database, reachable by the same execute_sql tool used to read tickets.

Customers write ticket messages through the public support widget, and rows in support_messages are shown back to the customer, making support_messages both an untrusted input source and a customer-visible egress sink.
The IDE client asks for approval on every tool call and shows the SQL, but developers approve many calls per session, the approval-fatigue pattern that degrades even a raw-action review gate.

recommendations.action: Replace the service-role Supabase connection with a least-privilege database role that enforces row level security and has no access to the integration_tokens table.
Add an output content filter on inserts to customer-visible tables such as support_messages, blocking writes containing credential-shaped strings before they reach the customer.

Treat retrieved ticket text as untrusted: delimit it explicitly, add an injection classifier before planning, and require a second, higher-friction approval when ticket-derived content requests a cross-table read or a write beyond the originating ticket.
Log every execute_sql call with SQL text, approving developer identity, and timestamp to a tamper-evident store independent of the agent's own output.
Cap raw-SQL approvals per developer per session and require a distinct destination confirmation before any write to a customer-visible table.

findings.title: Unpinned MCP server version (@latest) enables tool-definition rug pull (ASI04)

forecast.watch_signal: Package version pinned (or not) in config diffs when the Supabase MCP server dependency is updated; monitor npm supply-chain advisories for this package.

evidence.observation: The MCP server is launched via 'npx -y @supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest', which re-resolves to the newest published version on every invocation with no version pin or integrity check.

recommendations.action: Pin the Supabase MCP server to an exact, reviewed version (not @latest) and verify package integrity (checksum or lockfile) before each install.
Monitor the pinned package for upstream version changes and re-review tool descriptions and schemas on every update before approving the new version.

findings.title: No attributable record of agent-executed SQL separating agent action from developer approval (repudiation gap)

forecast.watch_signal: No tamper-evident logging introduced as autonomy increases or session volume grows, widening the gap between agent actions and attributable identity.

evidence.observation: No logging, audit trail, or provenance mechanism is described anywhere in the configuration or runtime notes for execute_sql calls, despite the tool being able to read restricted data and write customer-visible replies.

recommendations.action: Implement tamper-evident audit logging of agent-executed database actions tied to the approving developer identity, independent of agent-controlled output.

findings.title: No spend, rate, or step limit on execute_sql reads/writes beyond per-call human approval

forecast.watch_signal: Approval gate removed or loosened, or autonomy raised beyond per-step approval, removing the only throttle currently on SQL execution volume.

evidence.observation: The only described throttle on tool execution is per-call human approval ('developers approve many calls in a session'); no spend cap, rate limit, or step limit is described for execute_sql reads or writes.

recommendations.action: Add a hard per-session or per-hour cap on execute_sql calls, independent of human approval, to bound cost and blast radius if approvals are rubber-stamped.

stride_coverage.rationale: Artifacts do not describe how the agent's own identity is authenticated to other systems or whether it could be impersonated beyond the static access token used for the MCP server.
This is an inbound flow carrying customer-authored text into the agent; it does not itself move data outward, so information disclosure does not apply to this direction of flow.
Artifacts do not describe any rate limiting or protection against a flood of ticket submissions through the public support widget.
Denial of service risk from unbounded invocation volume is captured at the capability level in find.no_spend_rate_limit; this single bounded insert flow doesn't add a distinct vector.

rating.rationale: The design connects an untrusted source (customer-authored ticket text, submitted through an unauthenticated public widget) to a service-role database connection that bypasses row level security and can read a table of integration tokens, and then to a customer-visible write (TC1 lethal trifecta). Inherent risk is critical. The only control is a per-call human approval prompt that shows raw SQL; because developers approve many calls per session (approval fatigue, SAFE-T1403/ASI09), its credit is capped at one tier and residual cannot be driven below moderate, leaving residual at high. Forecast is critical: removing or loosening that gate (autonomy_increase, control_removal) reopens the full inherent path. Two further gaps compound the picture: the Supabase MCP server is pulled unpinned (@latest), so its tool definitions can change without review (ASI04, high); and there is no attributable audit log of agent actions and no spend/rate/step limit beyond the same approval prompt, so a rogue or fatigued-approval session is both unaccountable and unbounded. The approval gate's decay under volume is the single control most responsible for the gap between residual and forecast.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration (mcp.json and runtime notes) provided for review, not observed runtime behavior; actual approval compliance, logging, and query scoping may differ in production.

No MCP server tool schema or source code was provided, so the exact parameters of execute_sql and whether its scope can be restricted are inferred from runtime notes; confidence on capability boundaries is medium.
No system prompt or orchestration instructions were provided, so the instructions review (ambiguous goals, conflicting directives) could not be performed.
No information was provided on logging or observability infrastructure; the audit-trail finding is based on the absence of any mention, which is weaker evidence than a confirmed absence.
